content: Patients must be informed that their discussions with healthcare providers regarding contraception are strictly confidential. There is currently insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness and feasibility of midwives diagnosing preterm pre-labour rupture of membranes (pPROM) and administering initial treatment with injectable antibiotics using a standard syringe prior to referral. However, this intervention may be both acceptable and feasible, and it has the potential to reduce healthcare inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. It is recommended that this option be considered within the framework of targeted monitoring and evaluation. This intervention should be implemented in settings where midwives are already an established cadre and where a well-functioning referral system is either in place or can be established. When shifting tasks from one cadre of healthcare workers to another, planners must address several critical factors. These include the distribution of roles among cadres, regulatory considerations, stakeholder involvement, training and supervision, referral systems, supply chains, and potential changes to payment structures or other incentives. For this intervention, programmes must ensure that it promotes continuity of care and that all midwives are adequately trained to deliver this task to all eligible recipients. Midwives and their supervisors should receive appropriate initial and ongoing training, including communication with patients and managing the side effects of various contraceptive methods. Training must emphasize that midwives should not introduce their own criteria when determining who should receive contraception. In addition to training midwives on confidentiality-related issues, patients must also be made aware that their interactions with healthcare workers regarding contraception are confidential. There is insufficient evidence on the effectiveness of midwives performing external cephalic version (ECV), and this intervention has the potential to cause harm. However, it is likely to be acceptable and feasible and may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. It is suggested that this option be considered in the context of rigorous research. Midwives administering corticosteroids to pregnant women for fetal neuroprotection in the context of preterm labour is another area with insufficient evidence. While this intervention may be feasible, its acceptability remains uncertain. It may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. This option should be considered within the framework of rigorous research. The effectiveness of midwives performing vacuum extraction during childbirth is also uncertain, and the acceptability of this intervention is unclear. However, it is likely to be feasible and may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. This option should be considered with targeted monitoring and evaluation of failure rates, complications, and process measures such as frequency of use. Midwives delivering a loading dose of magnesium sulfate to prevent eclampsia and referring patients to higher-level facilities is supported by a WHO guideline in settings where the full magnesium sulfate regimen cannot be administered. This guideline recommends a loading dose followed by immediate transfer for women with severe pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. However, the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low quality, and the recommendation is weak. This option should be considered within the context of targeted monitoring and evaluation. The administration of a maintenance dose of magnesium sulfate by midwives to prevent eclampsia and referral to higher-level facilities is another area with insufficient evidence. While this intervention may be feasible and acceptable under certain conditions, its acceptability is uncertain. It may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. This option should be considered within the context of targeted monitoring and evaluation. Midwives delivering magnesium sulfate to women in preterm labour as a neuroprotective intervention for the fetus is an area with insufficient evidence. However, midwives possess the necessary clinical skills for diagnosing preterm labour and administering magnesium sulfate, making this intervention potentially acceptable and feasible. This option should be considered within the context of rigorous research. The insertion and removal of intrauterine devices (IUDs) by auxiliary nurse midwives and nurses is supported by evidence suggesting that they can perform these tasks effectively. This intervention is likely feasible and may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. It is recommended that this option be implemented in settings with well-functioning midwifery programmes. The performance of tubal ligation by midwives is an area with insufficient evidence. However, this intervention may be an acceptable and feasible approach to contraception and may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations. This option should be considered within the context of rigorous research. The performance of external cephalic version (ECV) by associate clinicians is outside their typical scope of practice, and its acceptability and feasibility are uncertain. There is insufficient evidence to support this intervention, and it is recommended against. The performance of vacuum extraction during childbirth by associate clinicians is also outside their typical scope of practice, and its acceptability and feasibility are uncertain. There is insufficient evidence to support this intervention, and it is recommended against. The administration of a loading dose of magnesium sulfate by associate clinicians to prevent eclampsia and referral to higher-level facilities is supported by a WHO guideline in settings where the full magnesium sulfate regimen cannot be administered. However, this intervention is outside their typical scope of practice, and its acceptability is uncertain. It is recommended against. The performance of caesarean sections by associate clinicians is an area with insufficient evidence. The feasibility of this intervention is uncertain in many settings, as associate clinicians generally lack surgical skills. It is recommended against. The manual removal of the placenta by associate clinicians is another area with insufficient evidence. The feasibility of this intervention is uncertain in many settings, as associate clinicians generally lack surgical and manual obstetric skills. However, this intervention has the potential to reduce inequalities by extending vital healthcare to underserved populations. This option should be considered with targeted monitoring and evaluation. Advanced-level associate clinicians performing external cephalic version (ECV) is an area with insufficient evidence. While this intervention may be feasible and may reduce inequalities by extending care to underserved populations, its acceptability is uncertain.
